corrected_value.authors: Derwing, T. M., & Munro, M. J.
corrected_value.title: Accent, intelligibility, and comprehensibility: Evidence from four L1s.

decision.quote: Abstract This study investigated the relationship among intelligibility, comprehensibility, and accentedness in the speech of second language learners of Spanish of varying proficiency in instructed contexts. It conceptually replicated studies by Munro and Derwing (1995a) and Derwing and Munro (1997), who found partial independence among the three speech dimensions but also evidence that proficiency may mediate the relationship between linguistic features of stimuli (e.g., phonemic and grammatical error rates) and speech dimensions.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The abstract explicitly states that the study conceptually replicated both Munro and Derwing (1995a) and Derwing and Munro (1997), specifically retesting their findings of partial independence among intelligibility, comprehensibility, and accentedness and proficiency mediation of the relationship between linguistic error rates and speech dimensions using new speech data from 42 L2 Spanish learners rated by 80 native Spanish listeners. The supplied publisher reference list provides the full bibliographic identity for Derwing and Munro (1997) in Studies in Second Language Acquisition (19, 1-16, DOI 10.1017/S0272263197001010), confirmed in Crossref metadata. Shipped row 1267 (Munro & Derwing, 1995, Language Learning, 45, 73-97, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-1770.1995.tb00963.x) matches sibling target_index 0; Derwing and Munro (1997) is a separate subsequent empirical study across four L1s rather than an alternate report of the 1995 paper, and is genuinely absent from the shipped rows.

decision.quote: An initial study analyzing two small‐scale field experiments argued that describing someone as a voter (noun) instead of one who votes (verb) increases turnout rates 11 to 14 points because the noun activates a person's social identity as a voter. decision.quote:
Our hypotheses attempted to replicate Roozenbeek et al.’s (2021)
ﬁndings. Roozenbeek et al. tested whether prompting people to
think about accuracy reduced their willingness to share misinfor-
mation and/or increased their willingness to share true information
related to COVID-19 generally. They found the accuracy nudge
decreased intentions to share misinformation but did not signiﬁ-
cantly increase intentions to share true information. Our ﬁndings
are in partial agreement with Roozenbeek and colleagues. The
accuracy nudge did not decrease willingness to share false general
COVID-19 information in Kyrgyzstan or the United States. In India,
the accuracy nudge did decrease willingness to share general
COVID-19 misinformation.

decision.quote: In this article, Salomon's model and the research in which the model was tested are discussed, and a replication study is presented. The study determines the internal structure of the Dutch versions of Salomon's instruments and tests some predictions following from the model. Unlike their American peers, Dutch children do not unconditionally perceive television as an easy medium.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The supplied primary source contains only the publisher landing-page abstract and reference list for Beentjes (1989). The abstract states that it presents a Dutch replication study determining the internal structure of Dutch versions of Salomon's instruments, testing predictions from Salomon's (1981) model, and comparing Dutch children's media perceptions to those of their American peers. However, the abstract does not cite which empirical study is replicated, and the reference list contains two distinct 1984 empirical articles on children's media perceptions and effort investment: Salomon (1984), 'Television is "easy" and print is "tough": The differential investment of mental effort in learning as a function of perceptions and attributions' (Journal of Educational Psychology, 74, 647-658), and Salomon & Leigh (1984), 'Predispositions about learning from print and television' (Journal of Communication, 34, 119-135), the latter of which is shipped row 1863 (DOI 10.1111/j.1460-2466.1984.tb02164.x). Without the article body, the evidence cannot resolve whether the retested target is already represented by shipped row 1863, is Salomon (1984), or includes both.
